variants.name: async/await fan-out joined by Promise.all (ES2017)
variants.implementation_notes: JavaScript has one event loop per realm, so the master's dispatch is task creation and the join is a combinator: Promise.all(parts) resolves with the partials in input order and rejects on the first failure while the siblings keep running (use allSettled for quorum or partial-result semantics). That is genuine concurrency for I/O-bound sub-tasks but not parallelism - a CPU-bound sub-task blocks the loop and every other sub-task with it. Bound the fan-out (a limiter or chunked batches) because launching thousands of promises adds queue pressure rather than throughput, and treat a rejection as an error report, not a cancellation: stragglers must be aborted explicitly if that is wanted.
pitfalls: The first rejection wins while the other sub-tasks keep running: half-updated state and leaked work unless the tasks are abortable or allSettled is used.
One Promise.all over a huge input keeps every task and partial in memory at once - chunk the dispatch or cap in-flight tasks.
A CPU-heavy task starves the event loop, so timers, I/O and all sibling sub-tasks stall; use worker threads for compute.

variants.name: Pre-warmed worker_threads pool with a request/response protocol (Node.js)
variants.idiom_name: pool of node:worker_threads Workers + per-job promises
variants.implementation_notes: For CPU-bound sub-tasks the workers must be real threads: create a fixed pool of Worker instances once, post job payloads to idle workers, and resolve one promise per job from the pool's queue. The Node documentation is explicit that spawning a Worker per task costs more than the task and that a pool should be used (it also points at AsyncResource for correlating tasks in diagnostics). Data crosses by structured clone or transfer, so large inputs should be transferred as ArrayBuffers, and SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics is the only way to share mutable memory - which ends the 'identical independent workers' assumption. Shutdown is the pool's protocol (terminate or a close message), not a per-task signal; a worker that exits or crashes must be replaced and its in-flight job rejected or requeued.
pitfalls: Creating a Worker per sub-task dwarfs the work (the docs recommend a pool), and pool size must track the core count or the tasks oversubscribe the machine.
Structured clone copies inputs and outputs; transferring buffers neuters the sender's view and shared mutation requires SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics.
Worker errors and exit codes arrive as events, not exceptions: a crashed worker must be replaced and its job resolved or requeued, and stack traces do not cross the boundary.
